newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi high court to rule on Liggett papers.
newsitem.headline: Mississippi high court to rule on Liggett papers.

text.p: Attorneys for the tobacco industry have asked the Mississippi Supreme Court to block the release Friday of internal documents from the Liggett Group, papers filed with the court showed.

The nine-judge Supreme Court is being asked to overturn an order issued in Jones County Circuit Court that would allow plaintiffs in a $650 million second-hand-smoke case against cigarette makers to see 11 documents from Liggett, a Brooke Group Ltd subsidiary.
The documents are scheduled to be released at 1700 EST today.
An appeal of the lower court ruling, which if left standing could effectively make the secret Liggett documents public, was filed with the Supreme Court late yesterday.
Court officials said Supreme Court judges began reviewing the documents Thursday evening.

The documents are among the records that Liggett agreed to turn over last week in a settlement with 22 states that are suing the tobacco industry to recoup an estimated $30 billion in Medicaid funds spent treating people for smoking-related illnesses.
Jones County Circuit Judge Billy Joe Landrum ruled Wednesday that the documents could be turned over to attorneys for the family of Burl Butler, a Mississippi barber who died of cancer in 1994.
The family contends that Butler, who was 60 and never smoked, died of second-hand smoke from the cigarettes, cigars and pipes of people who patronized his shop over the course of 30 years.
The suit alleges that cigarette makers knew of the dangers of smoking but concealed the information. Plaintiffs say the Liggett papers may contain information to back up that claim.
When Landrum made his ruling, he also issued a stay so that tobacco industry lawyers would have until 1700 EST/2200 GMT today to secure a decision from the high court.
The appeal was submitted by two attorneys, including former Mississippi Supreme Court Justice Reuben Anderson.
"The circuit court's order threatens petitioners with immediate, irreversible harm by disclosure of information protected by the attorney-client privilege," the appeal said.
Landrum concluded the documents were outside the scope of attorney-client privilege because they included statements by industry experts who were not meant to testify at trial.
